messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At nineteen, Emily had been married less than a year when she was assaulted, and she still describes her life as divided into before and after. The assault happened at night as she was walking back from a convenience store near her apartment. She remembers hearing a motorcycle idling nearby before it came closer, and then men’s voices, one of them suddenly raised in Arabic. The sharp smell of alcohol hit her before she fully understood what was happening. What stayed with her most was the combination of those sensations—the engine noise, the shouting, the stale liquor on someone’s breath—so that the event now lives in her as much through sound and smell as through images.

In the weeks afterward, those cues began to pull the memory back with shocking speed. A motorcycle passing her street could bring back the whole scene without warning, and if she heard men shouting in Arabic from a passing car or from a phone video somewhere in public, she would freeze and feel the assault rush back in full force. When the memory came, she did not just think about what happened; she heard the voices in her head as if they were happening again and sometimes caught the smell of alcohol so vividly that she would look around to see where it was coming from. Over time, the memories themselves seemed to make the world more densely packed with danger cues. She had become so sensitized to engine noise, raised male voices, and the smell of liquor that she noticed them everywhere, and ordinary surroundings began to feel littered with traps.

Emily came to believe that what happened had destroyed her basic assumptions about how the world worked. Before the assault, she said, she had assumed that if she was careful and did the right things, she would be safe; now she was certain that safety could vanish instantly and for no reason. She also judged herself harshly. She was convinced that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, that another woman would have fought back, run faster, or somehow known what to do. Hearing a motorcycle rev or catching alcohol on a stranger’s breath did not just trigger fear; it also brought a flood of self-condemning thoughts about being weak and no longer capable, as if those sensations proved again that she had been changed into someone less competent than she used to be.

Those beliefs fed directly into the way she now watches for danger. She listens at home for any sound that might mean someone is entering, especially at night, and she checks behind her repeatedly when she does go out, certain that if she misses one sign she will be caught off guard again. What frightened her most was not only the possibility of another assault but the conviction that she would fail again if something happened. When she had a flashback, that sense of present danger intensified; her body reacted as if the assault were happening again, and she would scan doors, windows, and hallways with desperate concentration. The more she monitored for threat, the more easily fragments of the assault broke through—voices, the engine, the smell—and each recurrence seemed to confirm for her that the world was unsafe and that she was no longer able to manage it.

Her avoidance developed gradually but has become the structure of her days. She refuses to go out after dark, because nighttime feels inseparable from what happened and because every motorcycle or distant shout seems amplified once the sun goes down. She avoids dates connected to the assault, becoming tense and withdrawn as they approach, staying home and trying not to think about the calendar. She also avoids looking at or paying attention to her own body; even catching her reflection while dressing can stir up the memory too abruptly. At first these strategies felt like the only way to prevent being overwhelmed, but they have narrowed her life. Because she is unemployed, much of her time is spent inside the apartment, where she tries to control what she hears and smells, yet that has made her more reactive when she does encounter those cues. The more thoroughly she organizes life around avoiding night, anniversaries, and her own body, the less chance she has to learn that a motorcycle passing by or alcohol on someone in a grocery line is not the assault happening again. Instead, each avoidance seems to preserve the rawness of the memory and strengthen her belief that she cannot cope.

Her husband has become used to finding her checking the locks repeatedly or pausing mid-conversation because she has heard a sound outside. She knows how young she is to feel this defeated, and that thought shames her further. By the time she sought help, she was spending most evenings braced for danger, scanning for noises, and dreading sudden sensory jolts that could pull her back into the assault. She came in because she feels her world shrinking and because she is terrified that this is permanent—that she will always live as if the next motorcycle, the next shouted phrase, or the next trace of alcohol means she is back there again.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state that intrusive trauma memories themselves lead to or increase triggers/reminders, rather than simply making her notice danger cues more often.
There is no paragraph explicitly conveying that her sense of threat causes or intensifies negative appraisals/beliefs, as opposed to beliefs feeding threat.
The vignette does not explicitly describe avoidance or other maladaptive strategies as causing or increasing triggers/reminders.
The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies themselves increase her sense of threat, even though they preserve memory rawness and beliefs about not coping.
